name: Conversion / lifecycle marketing triggers (event-driven journeys)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Conversion and lifecycle marketing triggers / event-driven customer journeys
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A growth / lifecycle / CRM engineering team needs to fire an email, push, SMS, in-app, or webhook the moment a per-user behavioral counter crosses a threshold ('viewed product N times in 24h', 'cart-abandoned 30 min after add-to-cart', 'no login in 14 days', '3 failed checkouts in 1 hour'), with end-to-end freshness measured in seconds, not the 5–60 minute lag that warehouse-resident or batch reverse-ETL trigger flows ship today.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Browse / cart / checkout abandonment recovery: detect 'user added-to-cart and did not purchase within 30–60 min' and fire a Braze / Iterable / Customer.io / Klaviyo journey within seconds — the published industry benchmark is that recovery messages sent within 1 hour convert at ~20% vs. ~12% after 24 hours, so freshness is directly tied to recovered revenue. 2) Engagement / aha-moment triggers: 'user did core_event N times in 24h' or 'user finished step 3 of onboarding but not step 4 within 48h' to fire onboarding nudges, lifecycle email tracks, or in-app prompts. 3) Re-engagement and churn save: 'no session in 7/14/30 days' or 'usage dropped >50% vs. trailing 7d baseline' to fire winback campaigns. 4) Real-time consent / suppression / frequency-cap state: per-user 'messages_today', 'last_message_ts', 'do_not_disturb_until' counters that the journey engine must read before firing the next message. 5) Cross-channel orchestration signals: per-(user, channel) counters that decide email-vs-push-vs-SMS-vs-in-app routing based on which channel the user has interacted with most recently.
domain_fit.event_shapes: Standard behavioral / commerce events typically published by Segment / RudderStack / Snowplow / mParticle / first-party SDKs: page_view {ts, user_id, anonymous_id, url, session_id, device}, product_viewed {ts, user_id, sku, category, price}, add_to_cart {ts, user_id, sku, qty, cart_value}, checkout_started {ts, user_id, cart_value, items[]}, purchase / order_completed {ts, user_id, order_id, amount, currency}, signup {ts, user_id, plan, source}, feature_used {ts, user_id, feature_name}, login {ts, user_id, device}, message_sent / message_opened / message_clicked {ts, user_id, channel, campaign_id} (the engagement-feedback loop). Plus identify {anonymous_id -> user_id} so pre-auth browse state can be stitched onto the user record at signup.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of count, n_unique, recency, and velocity primitives in sliding and session windows: count(add_to_cart, 30m / 1h / 24h), count(product_viewed, 24h / 7d), n_unique(sku_viewed, 24h), recency(last_purchase_ts), recency(last_login_ts), recency(last_message_sent_ts), velocity(events_per_minute), distance(session_count_7d, session_count_baseline_28d) for churn-risk deltas, time_since(checkout_started) without subsequent purchase (the cart-abandonment indicator), session-window primitives for 'is_in_active_session' gating, and per-(user, channel) counters for frequency capping (messages_sent_today_email, messages_sent_today_push). Funnel-step features (max-seen onboarding_step, time_since_step_N) drive aha-moment and onboarding triggers. Distribution / top-K of recently-viewed categories drives recommendation-style trigger personalization.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite. user_id (authenticated) is the dominant key; anonymous_id covers pre-auth browse and abandonment; (user_id, channel) for frequency caps; (user_id, campaign_id) and (user_id, journey_id) for journey-engine de-dupe and exit-criteria; (user_id, sku) and (user_id, category) for product-level abandonment; (account_id / workspace_id) for B2B. Identity stitching at the identify event (anonymous_id -> user_id) is load-bearing — pre-signup browse counters must survive sign-up or the welcome journey misfires.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: All three plus thresholding. Sliding windows are the workhorse for 'did X N times in last Y' threshold tests (typically minutes-to-72-hours). Session windows (~30 min inactivity on web, ~5 min on mobile) drive 'still-in-session' personalization gates and the canonical cart-abandonment definition. Tumbling windows drive daily/hourly frequency caps and engagement reports. Approximate aggregates (HLL for unique-product-viewed counts, CMS / Top-K for hot categories) are acceptable for personalization triggers but exact counts are required where the counter is a frequency-cap contract ('max 3 emails per 24h'). The defining additional primitive vs. behavioral analytics (use case 5) is the trigger / fire-on-threshold-cross action — the buyer wants the side effect, not the read.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once is acceptable for most behavioral triggers (a duplicate add_to_cart counter increment will not fire a duplicate journey if Braze / Iterable / Customer.io de-dupe on event_id at their side, which they do). Exactly-once / strict idempotency does become load-bearing for (a) frequency caps that are part of a regulatory contract (CAN-SPAM / GDPR consent budgets) and (b) message-firing itself, where double-firing a $50 SMS or a sensitive transactional email is a real cost. The journey engine is the system of record for firing; beava is the threshold-detection engine, and event_id-keyed idempotency at ingest is sufficient there.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Read p99 <10–50 ms for trigger-decision reads from the journey engine; total event-to-fire end-to-end target is single-digit seconds (incumbents publish 'seconds' for streaming triggers — Hightouch Event Streaming claims 'events stream in seconds', Segment Engage real-time computed traits update on event arrival). For cart-abandonment use cases the trigger latency budget is governed by the abandonment window itself (15–60 min is the published optimal), so the threshold-cross detection just needs to be 'in time' rather than sub-second. beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get/batch_get sits inside the read budget; the open question is the fire-on-threshold side, which beava v0 does not ship.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to a few seconds end-to-end is the differentiating goal vs. the warehouse-resident stack. Public reference points: Segment Engage real-time computed traits update on event arrival; Hightouch Streaming Reverse ETL targets ~1 minute minimum lag with Snowflake Dynamic Tables (raw streams in seconds); Adobe RTCDP streaming segmentation publishes up to 5 minutes to qualify and 15+ minutes through the CDP layer for non-edge data; Census / Hightouch batch reverse-ETL syncs are typically 5–60 min cadence; Snowflake / BigQuery + dbt counter refreshes are 5–60 min. beava's push-on-event, no-broker model targets sub-second, which is exactly the 'fresh-enough to fire while the user is still in-session' gap that this domain is built around.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state EPS for a typical mid-market lifecycle marketer is in the 1k–50k EPS range; enterprise B2C is higher. Public reference: Braze processed 25.8 trillion data points across its platform in 2025 and is sized to handle ~400k requests/second at the API tier and 'billions of events per hour'; per-tenant single-customer rates vary widely but a 10M-MAU Klaviyo / Braze / Iterable tenant typically lands in low-to-mid five-figure EPS. A single beava node at ~684k EPS (M4, TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) comfortably covers a single mid-to-large lifecycle-marketing tenant. Multi-tenant SaaS deployments would still need horizontal partitioning (which beava v0 does not provide). [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Balanced-to-write-heavy. Every behavioral event is a write; reads happen when the journey engine evaluates trigger conditions and when frequency-cap / suppression state is queried before firing. Once triggers fire on threshold-cross internally (instead of being polled), the workload tips toward write-heavy because the journey engine no longer polls every user every minute. In a polling architecture (the common deployment today on top of warehouse-resident counters) the read-to-write ratio is artificially inflated by trigger-polling traffic.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by user_id and anonymous_id cardinality. A typical mid-market lifecycle marketer has 1M–50M addressable contacts plus 5–10x that in anonymous_ids per year. At ~300–600 B per per-entity rolling-feature vector (a handful of counters + recency timestamps + per-channel frequency-cap state + a few funnel-step max-seen values), 10M active entities is ~3–6 GB and 100M is ~30–60 GB. Frequency-cap state per (user, channel) adds 4–8x multiplication on the user count but each cell is tiny. Anonymous_id explosion (cookie / mobile-ad-id churn) is the dominant operational risk; aggressive TTL eviction (24–72h on unstitched anonymous_id, longer on stitched user_id) is mandatory. Most tenants land at single-digit-to-low-tens of GB hot state — fits in RAM on a single modern box. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Slowly-growing on user_id (bounded by addressable contact list). Explosive on anonymous_id (browser cookie churn, mobile ad-id resets). Bounded on channel (~5–10: email, push, sms, in-app, webhook, slack, whatsapp). Bounded on campaign_id and journey_id (low thousands per tenant). Bounded on event_name (tens to low hundreds). The (user_id, sku) and (user_id, category) cross-products are bounded by catalog size, which is bounded for most buyers (10k–10M SKUs) but pathological for very large marketplaces.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Minutes-to-hours for abandonment / in-session triggers (cart abandonment is the canonical 30–60 min window). 24–72 hours for short-window engagement triggers ('did X N times in 24h'). 7–30 days for re-engagement / churn-save triggers ('no login in 14d'). 30–365 days for cohort and LTV-bucket features. Frequency-cap counters tumble daily / weekly / monthly. Anonymous_id state should TTL aggressively (24–72 h) unless stitched.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 3–15 features per trigger evaluation (vs. 20–100+ for fraud). A typical journey-engine step reads a handful of counters (events_in_window, last_event_ts, frequency_cap_state, journey_state) and a couple of recency timestamps. Re-evaluating a multi-branch journey may batch 30–100 feature reads per user.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe. Losing 5 minutes of behavioral counters on restart will miss a few cart-abandonment fires but does not produce a financial, regulatory, or audit error. The hard durability constraint is on frequency-cap state and consent state — over-firing a regulated channel (CAN-SPAM, GDPR consent withdrawal, TCPA SMS) is a real liability. beava's WAL + snapshot is sufficient for the behavioral side; the consent / frequency-cap-of-record needs additional invariants (atomic increment-on-fire, no-double-count) which beava's atomic-per-push semantics support but the buyer will want documented.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Strong fit for single-binary sidecar-next-to-event-collector and per-tenant-in-SaaS topologies. A growth team can run beava as a single sidecar next to their Segment / RudderStack / Snowplow / first-party collector and have the journey engine (Braze / Iterable / Customer.io / Klaviyo) call beava for trigger-condition evaluation. A composable-CDP vendor (Hightouch, Census) could embed beava as the per-tenant 'hot trigger tier' behind their streaming destinations. Multi-region active-active is occasionally required for global tenants but most lifecycle marketing is region-affinity-tolerant. The hard limit is in-process sharding (beava v0 lacks it) for a single very large tenant exceeding ~684k EPS or tens of GB of hot state.

commercial_fit.who_buys: (a) Growth / lifecycle marketing engineering teams at SaaS, e-commerce, fintech, gaming, media — the engineers behind the Braze / Iterable / Customer.io / Klaviyo deployment. (b) CRM / marketing-platform teams at large brands building 'composable CDP' stacks on top of Snowflake / Databricks / BigQuery with Hightouch or Census as the activation layer. (c) Mid-market e-commerce teams running Klaviyo or Customer.io who feel the freshness gap on cart abandonment and want a self-hosted hot-counter layer between their event collector and their journey engine. (d) Self-hosting buyers running open-source Customer.io alternatives (Dittofeed, Laudspeaker, LimeJourney, Mautic) who need a real-time counter store to drive triggers without Redis-plus-Lua. (e) Vendors themselves (lifecycle / CDP / reverse-ETL) who might embed beava as the per-tenant hot counter tier behind their managed product.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: The customer engagement / lifecycle marketing market is large and well-funded. The customer engagement solutions market is sized at ~$24B in 2025 growing to ~$57–86B by 2034 (Fortune Business Insights, Precedence Research) at 10% CAGR. The adjacent CDP market is sized at ~$9–10B in 2025 growing to ~$37B by 2030 at ~30% CAGR (MarketsandMarkets). Public-comparable revenue: Klaviyo did $1.2B in FY2025 (32% YoY), Braze did ~$700M run-rate (Q3 FY2026 revenue $190.8M, ~25% YoY growth), Iterable was valued at $2B on ~$240M revenue in 2024, and Customer.io is private but in the same growth bracket. The composable-CDP entrants (Hightouch, Census) are growing nearly 13% in headcount per CMSWire and Hightouch was named Leader in the 2025 Gartner Magic Quadrant for CDPs. Frequency-cap / journey-decisioning / real-time-streaming triggers are an explicit shared roadmap line item across all of these vendors. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) The 'streaming reverse ETL' moment — Hightouch (Streaming Reverse ETL, Event Streaming), Census, RudderStack, Adobe RTCDP are all racing to close the 5–60 min reverse-ETL latency gap that warehouse-resident lifecycle journeys ship today. 2) Same-session personalization and in-session triggers (Algolia, Hightouch, Bloomreach, Contentful are all publishing on the 200ms latency budget for real-time personalization in 2025–2026). 3) Cart-abandonment recovery economics: published benchmarks show ~20% recovery rate at <1h vs. ~12% at >24h, which directly motivates closing the warehouse-resident lag. 4) Per-event SaaS pricing pressure (Braze data-points, Klaviyo event-tier pricing, Iterable contracts) is pushing larger buyers to build hybrid stacks where the hot trigger tier is self-hosted. 5) Privacy regulation (GDPR Article 17 right-to-erasure, CCPA, Apple ATT, Google Privacy Sandbox) shortens identifier half-lives and forces in-region first-party processing — favors a single-binary in-region hot tier over a global SaaS counter. 6) AI-driven journey decisioning (Braze AI, Klaviyo AI, Iterable AI in 2025) needs fresher rolling behavioral features at the moment of decision.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: GDPR (Article 17 right-to-erasure with one-month response window, consent management, lawful basis for direct marketing — must cascade to all per-user counter state), CCPA / CPRA (same shape plus Do-Not-Sell flag must be honored before fire), CAN-SPAM (US email frequency / suppression list), TCPA (US SMS prior-express-consent and time-of-day rules), PECR (UK / EU electronic-marketing consent), Apple ATT and Google Privacy Sandbox (shrinking anonymous_id half-life). SOC 2 is table-stakes for any vendor selling to enterprise. Not regulator-grade durability (this is not AML), but PII handling matters: beava's lack of TLS / auth in v0 is a real blocker for any production deployment outside a strictly trusted VPC.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast — 1–3 days for a working 'cart-abandoned 30min ago' or 'did X 3 times in 24h' demo on a laptop wiring beava @bv.event + @bv.table to a Segment or Snowplow source and a Braze / Iterable / Customer.io webhook destination. 1–3 weeks to a production pilot in front of a single journey (typically cart-abandonment because the ROI is most legible), gated mostly by adding TLS / auth (the v0 gaps) and on building the trigger / fire-on-threshold primitive that beava does not ship today. Without the trigger primitive, the pilot has to poll beava from the journey engine on a cron — workable for a demo, suboptimal in production.

competition.incumbents: Generic real-time / streaming stack the buyer might assemble: Redis (counters + sorted sets + Lua scripts + EXPIRE for time-windows) is the overwhelming default for hot per-user lifecycle counters; Kafka + Flink (or Spark Real-Time Mode, Materialize, RisingWave) for stream-processed counters with windowed triggers; Snowflake Dynamic Tables / BigQuery streaming + dbt for warehouse-resident lifecycle counters with 1–60 min lag; Tecton / Hopsworks / Chalk / Fennel as managed online feature stores for lifecycle features; Postgres triggers + Redis counters + cron drift-heal jobs (which the beava README explicitly positions against). On the activation side, Hightouch (Event Streaming + Streaming Reverse ETL) and Census are the warehouse-native real-time activation layers.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Customer engagement / journey orchestration: Braze (NASDAQ:BRZE, Gartner MQ Leader 2025, real-time stream-processing engine, action-based delivery, ~25.8T data points / yr), Iterable ($2B valuation, ~$240M revenue), Customer.io, Klaviyo (NYSE:KVYO, $1.2B revenue 2025), MoEngage, CleverTap, Insider, OneSignal, Bloomreach Engagement, Sitecore Personalize, Adobe Journey Optimizer, Salesforce Marketing Cloud / Journey Builder, HubSpot Workflows. CDP layer: Segment (Twilio), RudderStack, mParticle (Rokt), Adobe RTCDP, Treasure Data, Tealium, Snowplow. Composable / warehouse-native CDP: Hightouch, Census. Open-source self-hosted alternatives to Customer.io / Braze: Dittofeed, Laudspeaker (YC), LimeJourney, Mautic. None of these is a pure feature server — they all bundle ingestion, identity stitching, schema, storage, journey UI, channel adapters, and activation. beava would naturally sit underneath one of these (powering the hot per-user counter tier behind triggers) rather than replace any of them outright.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Sub-second feature freshness for trigger evaluation vs. incumbents' published seconds-to-minutes (Hightouch Streaming 'seconds', Streaming Reverse ETL ~1 min, Adobe RTCDP up-to-5-min streaming segmentation, warehouse-resident dbt 5–60 min) — closes the cart-abandonment-recovery freshness gap that maps directly to recovered revenue. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives cover the count / n_unique / velocity / recency / distance / distribution features that lifecycle marketing literally lives on, without writing Lua-on-Redis or Flink SQL. 3) Single binary, no Kafka / Flink / Spark / Redis-cluster — fits a sidecar-next-to-collector or per-tenant-hot-tier embedding model. 4) Apache-2.0, no open-core — attractive to open-source Customer.io alternatives (Dittofeed, Laudspeaker, LimeJourney, Mautic) and to commercial vendors who might embed it. 5) Push-on-event over HTTP/JSON :8080 or framed TCP+msgpack :8081 maps directly to how Segment / RudderStack / Snowplow / first-party SDKs already produce events. 6) Recency / 'last-active' / 'time-since' and per-channel frequency-cap counters are first-class primitives, which on Redis are hand-rolled and on warehouses are simply too slow. 7) The beava README's own positioning ('Replaces Postgres triggers + Redis counters + the cron job that heals drift') is more or less describing this use case verbatim.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No trigger / fire-on-threshold primitive — this is the central missing piece for this domain. Today the buyer would poll beava from the journey engine on a per-second / per-minute cron, which works but is wasteful and adds latency. Without internal triggers, beava is a feature backend for triggers, not a trigger engine. 2) No TLS, no auth in v0 — disqualifying for any production SaaS deployment that handles PII / consent / suppression state (which is most of them); restricts beava today to in-VPC / behind-mTLS-proxy. 3) No in-process sharding — a single very large tenant (Klaviyo / Braze-class) must hand-shard externally. 4) No identity-stitch primitive (anonymous_id -> user_id at identify) — the buyer has to implement this on top, and getting it wrong leaks state across users. 5) No native consent / GDPR-tombstone primitive (atomic delete cascading all per-user counters) — must be implemented on top. 6) No native journey state machine — beava counts features, not journey-step transitions or 'has this user been in this journey before' state. 7) No multi-tenancy primitives (per-tenant namespaces, quotas, rate-limit accounting) for vendors embedding beava across customer workspaces. 8) No channel adapters — beava decides 'should fire', not 'how to deliver' (which is correct scope, but means it must compose with a downstream journey engine or channel system).
competition.integration_surface: Producers: web SDKs (Segment analytics.js, RudderStack JS, Snowplow, PostHog JS, Klaviyo onsite.js), mobile SDKs (Segment, Braze, Iterable, Customer.io, Amplitude, mParticle), server SDKs / webhooks (Shopify webhooks, Stripe webhooks, internal services), Kafka / Kinesis for buyers already on a streaming bus. beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 fits the SDK / webhook producer path with no shim. Consumers: lifecycle / journey engines (Braze action-based delivery / canvases, Iterable Journeys, Customer.io Campaigns, Klaviyo Flows, Mautic / Dittofeed / Laudspeaker / LimeJourney), composable-CDP activation layers (Hightouch Event Streaming + Streaming Reverse ETL, Census), in-house orchestrators (Temporal / Airflow / Kafka-Streams). The integration pattern is: 'something polls beava (today) or beava pushes (when triggers ship) -> journey engine -> channel SDK fires email / push / SMS / in-app / webhook'.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: External rules engine on the journey side (Braze canvases, Iterable workflows, Customer.io flows, Klaviyo flows, Adobe Journey Optimizer, in-house workflow engines like Temporal) reading beava features and deciding what to fire. ML scoring (propensity-to-purchase, churn-risk, channel-pick) is increasingly layered on top and would read per-user batch_get features from beava as part of feature inference. beava remains the pure feature backend; the journey engine is the rules engine, and the ML scorer is a separate concern.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public users of beava on this use case identified. [uncertain] Comparable production references at incumbents: Braze publicly cites 25.8T data points processed in 2025 and 'real-time stream-processing engine' for action-based delivery; Hightouch's Event Streaming and Streaming Reverse ETL launches name Braze / Iterable / Mixpanel as supported real-time destinations and cite cart-abandonment, onboarding, and lead-routing as canonical use cases; Segment Engage publishes real-time computed traits with session windows for instant personalization triggers; Klaviyo, Customer.io, MoEngage and CleverTap each publish abandoned-cart-flow case studies with documented uplift; the laudspeaker (YC) open-source launch explicitly positioned itself as 'Braze / Iterable / Customer.io alternative' with event-triggered cross-channel messaging; Dittofeed lists Customer.io / Klaviyo as displaced incumbents.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion threads identified on this topic. [uncertain] Broader community signal is strong: Hightouch's 'Reverse ETL 2.0: Streaming Is Here' announcement and changelog (2024), Hightouch Streaming Reverse ETL launch posts on LinkedIn and X, Klaviyo Community threads on abandoned-cart flow timing, Customer.io webhook-trigger documentation, Iterable Support Center threads on event-triggered journey behavior, r/marketing and r/dataengineering threads comparing Braze vs. Iterable vs. Customer.io, Hacker News threads on Klaviyo pricing and PostHog self-hosting, YC launch threads for Laudspeaker / Dittofeed / LimeJourney open-source alternatives.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No dedicated lifecycle-marketing-trigger demo identified in the repository. Adjacent reusable artifact: /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ (events.jsonl + schema.json with PageView / AddToCart / Purchase event shapes) — these are exactly the shapes a cart-abandonment / browse-abandonment trigger demo would consume. A purpose-built demo (cart_abandoned_30m, product_views_24h, time_since_last_purchase, messages_sent_today_email) would be a natural addition once a fire-on-threshold trigger primitive ships. The README's own framing ('Replaces Postgres triggers + Redis counters + the cron job that heals drift') is essentially the elevator pitch for this domain. [uncertain]
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Low / passive. There is no active adversary trying to evade or game the lifecycle counter — drift comes from product changes (new events, new journeys, new channels), schema evolution, and privacy mechanics (cookie / mobile-ad-id churn, consent revocation). This dramatically simplifies the operational story compared to fraud (use cases 1a–4) or anti-cheat (11). The buyer is allergic to outages (a missed cart-abandonment fire is missed revenue) and to over-firing (a duplicate message is brand damage and may breach CAN-SPAM / TCPA / GDPR consent), but tolerant of slightly approximate behavioral counts.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Replacing a lifecycle marketing tool's journey UI / channel adapters / template engine / send-time-optimization / deliverability infrastructure — beava is the trigger feature backend, not the journey engine or the channel sender. Braze / Iterable / Customer.io / Klaviyo own that surface. 2) Long historical lookback (>30–90 d) — beava is in-memory only; the warehouse remains the source for cohort / LTV / propensity training data. 3) Source-of-truth for consent / suppression / unsubscribe / preference center — that belongs in the journey engine or a dedicated consent registry (OneTrust, Transcend, dedicated identity service). beava can hold a per-user 'do_not_disturb_until' counter but must not be the system of record for legal consent. 4) Cross-entity SQL joins (user × campaign × journey × cohort × channel) for analyst reports — that is OLAP territory (Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse, Pinot). 5) Identity resolution / deterministic + probabilistic identity stitching at scale — beava can receive identify(anonymous_id -> user_id) and stitch state but is not a full ID-resolution provider (RudderStack Profiles, Segment Unify, mParticle IDSync, LiveRamp, Hightouch Profiles own that). 6) Channel delivery itself (SMTP, APNs/FCM, SMS gateways) — out of scope. 7) Send-time optimization, subject-line ML, content personalization — out of scope.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) Fire-on-threshold-cross triggers / 'when counter crosses N, POST a webhook or emit an internal event' — without this, the buyer must poll, which defeats the freshness pitch. This is the central gap, and it is explicitly called out in the use case description. The trigger primitive should support webhook fan-out (HTTP POST), deduplication so re-crossings within a window don't double-fire, and a documented at-least-once delivery contract with retry. 2) TLS termination and an auth model (token / mTLS) on :8081 and :8090 — without these, beava cannot hold user PII or consent state outside a strictly trusted VPC. 3) Identity stitching primitive: identify(anonymous_id -> user_id) that atomically merges all (anonymous_id, *) counters onto the user_id key with no double-counting and no state leak across identities. 4) Per-entity TTL / sliding-window eviction with a documented memory budget — anonymous_id cardinality is the dominant operational risk. 5) GDPR-style 'tombstone-by-user_id' primitive that cascades across all per-(user_id, *) features atomically, with a documented latency bound (regulator-friendly within one month is generous but most buyers want <1s). 6) Per-(user, channel) frequency-cap counters as a first-class concept with atomic-increment-on-fire semantics. 7) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting for vendors embedding beava across customer workspaces. 8) Schema evolution: lifecycle events change weekly; the @bv.event story needs to tolerate adding a new field without dropping state. 9) An optional event-archive sink (S3 / Parquet / Iceberg) so the cold tier can live alongside without forcing the buyer to dual-write. 10) In-process or sidecar sharding by user_id prefix for tenants that exceed a single box. 11) Documented exactly-once semantics for the trigger-fire path (so a webhook is delivered at most once per threshold-crossing) — the threshold-detection side can be at-least-once but the side-effect side should not double-fire a $50 SMS. 12) A small library of canonical journey-state primitives ('has-this-user-been-in-this-journey', 'last-message-sent-ts-by-channel') so the buyer does not reinvent them per tenant.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — this is the canonical use case where the trigger / fire-on-threshold-cross primitive is mandatory, not optional. Pure feature serving (read on poll) is workable for a demo but uneconomic in production: polling 5–15 features per user per minute across 10M users is wasteful, adds 30–60s of latency to the threshold detection, and forces the journey engine to own scheduling that beava could do for free. This is the largest single product gap for the domain, and shipping it would also unlock the lifecycle-marketing slice of use case 5 (behavioral analytics) and the alerting slice of use case 14 (observability).
